newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's inflation triumph marred by no growth.
newsitem.headline: Russia's inflation triumph marred by no growth.

text.p: Russia's government has managed to stamp out high inflation, but the collapse of output continues, and steady economic growth is not likely until next year, a Russian government expert said on Friday.

"Today one could say Russia's economy and society in general are entering an entirely new stage of their development -- life with low inflation," Sergei Pavlenko, head of the government's Centre for Economic Reform, told a news conference.

Consumer prices fell 0.2 percent in August -- the first fall since economic reforms began and prices were freed in 1992 -- after rising 0.7 percent in July, the State Statistics Committee said this week.
But Pavlenko said this figure was still preliminary.
"Our pessimistic forecast for inflation in August would be zero. The otpimistic one would be a 0.1 percent fall in prices," Pavlenko said.

He said low inflation was due not only to a seasonal fall in food prices, but largely to the authorities' determination to pursue a tight financial policy and the more stable political situation following the June and July presidential election.

"One should not underestimate the symbolism of zero inflation. Russian citizens have been convinced of the ability of their government and the president to fulfil promises to stamp out inflation," Pavlenko said.
Goskomstat said that if August prices trends continued, year-on-year inflation in December could be just 15 percent.
But Pavlenko said the authorities expected annual inflation of 18-19 percent this year due to expected rises in prices for electricity and other public services and utilities.
The government has so far targeted next year's annual inflation at 15 percent, but the figure could be reconsidered when the 1997 budget is adopted.
By slashing inflation "Russia has opened the door to economic growth", Pavlenko said but added the government has not managed to reverse the output collapse.
Gross domestic product (GDP) is now forecast to fall by one to two percent this year, he said.
"This is bad and means that the targeted GDP growth of 2.5 percent for this year can be achieved only next year," he said.
Pavlenko said yields on Treasury bills, still running at around 70 percent despite the slow-down in prices, would fall in line with inflation next year.
"It will be good if we reach the level of 30 percent annual by mid-1997, and if we reach 20 percent, it will be a victory," he said.
High yields make it more attractive for banks to invest short-term in government securities rather than in the real economy.
Economists largely blame the continuing decline in output on the high yields, which are stopping investment flowing into the productive sectors of the economy.
Until the government gets the budget deficit down, and interest rates fall, it will continue to corner the lion's share of available funds.

However many economists say official statistics, which show that GDP and industrial output in the first seven months of this year were both five percent lower than a year earlier, may be too gloomy, as they do not capture much of the private sector.

Pavlenko said that taking into account the shadow economy, where people are producing and trading but not paying taxes, the economy is probably already close to growth but it is impossible to measure this sector precisely.
